note: A woman, and half a village was drawn in a man's trousers until this file existed.

Long hair and a dress, which is what a village looked like from a distance for a thousand years and is the only version of this that survives being seen from up here. The rule is the miner's rule: the shape carries it, never the colour. Nothing below is a new colour — the dress takes the same palette entry the shirt does, so a woman is as many colours as a villager ever was, and what tells her apart is her outline.
Slighter than the man, at 0.9 against his 1.06. That is the trunk and the limbs and not the height: a woman is not a small man, and shrinking the whole figure would have made her a child.

Two cues rather than one, because one is a cue you lose the moment somebody turns round. From behind and from above it is the fall of hair; from the front and the side it is the hem, which is wider than her hips and wider than her shoulders and is the only wedge-shaped outline in the village.

parts.note: the fall of hair, down the back to the shoulder blades. Its top is buried inside the skull's own hair rather than resting on it — two faces at the same height fight for the same pixels and the head shimmers as the camera turns. It takes the same tint as the hair above it, so a fair woman is fair all the way down, and it turns with the head so it swings when she looks at you

the dress from the waist to the knee, a shade proud of the body so the two do not fight for the same pixels. Painted from the shirt's palette entry rather than a colour of its own, because a bodice and a skirt in two colours is a blouse and a skirt, and what is wanted is one garment

and its hem, wider than the skirt above it and wider than her shoulders: the flare is the whole silhouette, and it is what you read at the far end of a street. It stops at the knee rather than the ankle so the walk shows beneath it — the priest's cassock learnt that first — and so that she is never mistaken for him
